title: Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP/1.1): Message Syntax and Routing
summary: Gives an overview of HTTP architecture and terminology, defines the http and https URI schemes, and specifies the HTTP/1.1 message syntax, parsing requirements, and related security concerns. It was part of the RFC 7230 series that replaced RFC 2616. It was later replaced by RFC 9110 and RFC 9112.

eli5.summary: This is the rulebook for how web browsers and servers write their messages to each other, so both sides can read them. A newer rulebook has since taken its place.

questions: what is the http message syntax
http and https uri scheme definition
how does http determine message body length
subtitle: The text format of HTTP/1.1 messages, how they are framed, routed and carried over connections.

tldr.problem: Web clients, servers and intermediaries need one precise definition of how HTTP/1.1 messages are written, delimited, routed and carried over connections, or they will parse the same bytes differently.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7230 defines the http and https URI schemes, the start-line, header fields and body of a message, the rules for finding where a body ends (Content-Length, chunked coding, connection close), request-target and Host routing, and persistent connections.
tldr.outcome: It replaced RFC 2616 as the HTTP/1.1 message syntax document and has itself been obsoleted by RFC 9110 and RFC 9112.

today: RFC 7230 has been obsoleted by RFC 9110 and RFC 9112, and it was updated by RFC 8615. It obsoleted RFC 2616 and RFC 2145, so current work should follow the newer documents.

sections.title: HTTP Architecture and URI Schemes
sections.content:
HTTP is a stateless request/response protocol. A client opens a connection to a server and sends requests, and the server answers each with a response. The words client and server name roles on one connection, so the same program can be a client on one connection and a server on another. A user agent is any client that starts a request, such as a browser, spider, command-line tool or mobile app, and an origin server is the program that can give authoritative responses for a resource. The RFC points out that user agents and servers are not only browsers and big websites: it names household appliances, stereos, scales and home automation among them.

Messages look like Internet mail and MIME messages, and targets are identified with URIs. This RFC defines two schemes. An http URI names a potential origin server listening for TCP connections, with TCP port 80 as the default. An https URI is the same for TLS-secured connections, with port 443 as the default, and the user agent MUST make sure the connection is secured with strong encryption end-to-end before sending the first request. A sender MUST NOT generate an http URI with an empty host, and MUST NOT generate the deprecated userinfo part (user and password before an @) in a request target or header value.

Versions are written HTTP/major.minor. This document defines 1.1, and an HTTP/1.1 message sent to an HTTP/1.0 or unknown recipient is built so it could be read as valid HTTP/1.0 if the newer features were ignored.
sections.eli5: A browser asks, a server answers, and neither remembers the last conversation. The web address tells the browser whom to ask and whether to use a secret, locked channel.

sections.title: The Shape of an HTTP Message
sections.content:
Every HTTP/1.1 message is a start-line, zero or more header fields, an empty line, and an optional message body. The start-line is a request-line for requests or a status-line for responses.

A request-line is method SP request-target SP HTTP-version CRLF. The method is case-sensitive. Recipients of an invalid request-line SHOULD answer with 400 (Bad Request) or a 301 redirect to a properly encoded target, and SHOULD NOT silently fix it, since the line might be crafted to slip past security filters. All senders and recipients are RECOMMENDED to support request-lines of at least 8000 octets, and a server MUST answer 414 (URI Too Long) when the target is longer than it will parse.

A status-line is the version, a space, a 3-digit status code, a space and a reason phrase. A client SHOULD ignore the reason phrase, which exists only as a human-readable description.

Each header field is a case-insensitive name, a colon, optional whitespace, the value and optional trailing whitespace. A recipient MUST parse a message as octets in an encoding that is a superset of US-ASCII, because treating it as Unicode text can create security vulnerabilities. A sender MUST NOT put whitespace between the start-line and the first header field, since differing handling of that whitespace could be used to hide a field or a request.
sections.eli5: A message is like a form. The first line says what you want or how it went, then come labelled boxes with extra details, then a blank line, and finally the main content if there is any.

sections.title: Message Bodies and Knowing Where They End
sections.content:
Getting the end of a message right is central to the RFC, because a mistake lets a message be mistaken for two. A request has a body only when a Content-Length or Transfer-Encoding header says so. Responses to HEAD, all 1xx, 204 and 304 responses never have a body, and a 2xx response to CONNECT turns the connection into a tunnel.

For everything else the body length is decided in order of precedence. If Transfer-Encoding ends with chunked, the body is read and decoded until the chunked data is complete. If both Transfer-Encoding and Content-Length are present, Transfer-Encoding wins, and the message ought to be treated as an error because it may be a request smuggling or response splitting attempt. Conflicting or invalid Content-Length values make the framing invalid, and a server MUST answer 400 and close the connection. A valid Content-Length gives the number of octets. A request with neither has no body, and a response with neither is delimited by the server closing the connection. Servers SHOULD prefer length-delimited or encoded messages, because a closure-delimited message cannot be told apart from one cut short by a network failure.

The chunked transfer coding sends the body as a series of chunks, each with a hexadecimal size, followed by a last chunk of size zero, an optional trailer of header fields, and a final empty line. This lets a sender stream content of unknown size and still keep the connection open. Every recipient MUST be able to decode chunked.
sections.eli5: The receiver needs to know when a letter is over. Either the letter says how long it is, or it comes in numbered pieces ending with a piece marked zero. If the two instructions disagree, be suspicious.

sections.title: Request Targets and the Host Header
sections.content:
The request-target takes one of four forms depending on the method and whether the request goes to a proxy. origin-form is the absolute path plus optional query and is used when talking straight to an origin server. absolute-form is the full URI and is what a client MUST send to a proxy. authority-form is just the host and port and is only for CONNECT. asterisk-form is a single asterisk character and is only for a server-wide OPTIONS request.

Because many names can share one IP address, a client MUST send a Host header field in every HTTP/1.1 request. Its value is the authority of the target URI, without any userinfo, and it is empty if the URI has no authority. A user agent SHOULD put Host first after the request-line. Intermediaries are covered too: a Via header field records the proxies and gateways a message has passed through.
sections.eli5: One building can hold many shops. The Host line is the shop name on the envelope, so the doorman knows which shop the letter belongs to.

sections.title: Connections and Persistence
sections.content:
HTTP/1.1 connections are persistent by default, so one connection can carry many request/response exchanges. A recipient decides whether a connection persists from the version and Connection header of the most recent message. If close is present, the connection ends after the current response. Otherwise HTTP/1.1 or later persists, and HTTP/1.0 persists only if keep-alive is present and the recipient is not a proxy and chooses to honor it. A proxy MUST NOT keep a persistent connection with an HTTP/1.0 client.

To stay persistent, every message must have a length that does not depend on closing the connection. A server MUST read the whole request body or close the connection after responding, or the leftover bytes would be read as the next request. Client and server shut down cleanly with the close option: after sending or receiving it, no further requests may be sent or processed on that connection.

The RFC also covers retrying requests after a connection drops, pipelining several requests without waiting for responses, limits on concurrent connections, failures and timeouts, and the Upgrade header field for switching to another protocol.
sections.eli5: Keeping the phone line open lets you ask several questions in a row without redialing. Saying "close" means "I'm hanging up after this answer".

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC's security section covers establishing authority, risks of intermediaries, message integrity, confidentiality and the privacy of server logs. Several risks follow directly from the text-based format.

Parsers can be attacked by very long or very slow input where an element has no defined length, so the RFC gives minimum size recommendations and says recipients ought to limit how far they process methods, status phrases, field names, numbers and chunks, to avoid buffer overflows, arithmetic overflows and denial of service. Request smuggling exploits differences between parsers to hide extra requests inside a harmless one. This specification added new requirements on message framing, mainly the body length rules, to reduce its effectiveness. Response splitting is a related attack on how responses are delimited.
sections.eli5: If two people read the same letter and disagree about where it ends, a trickster can hide a second letter inside the first. The strict rules about letter length stop that.
